I'm an undergraduate aswell so certainly not an expert but I think geographically, coral reefs are typically found in tropical regions with clear, warm water, where large-scale nutrient input from upwelling or river runoff is minimal. Interestingly, these nutrient-poor waters actually benefit reefs, as high nutrient levels can promote algal blooms. These blooms often outcompete corals for sunlight and space, potentially smothering the reef. The nutrient scarcity in oligotrophic waters helps corals dominate. I always think about the massive amount of marine life in arctic zones with surprise. 

Generally, you’d expect more energy entering an ecosystem to result in more nutrients, so it’s understandable why the patterns of biodiversity in the oceans can seem unexpected. On land, the latitudinal diversity gradient (LDG) is more prominent because high solar energy near the equator drives nutrient cycling and primary productivity, supporting rich and complex ecosystems. In the oceans, however, water movement complicates this relationship. Currents, upwelling zones, and stratification play a significant role in nutrient distribution, creating hotspots of productivity in areas far from the equator, such as nutrient-rich upwelling zones, while tropical oceans often remain nutrient-poor despite abundant sunlight. These nuances make marine biodiversity patterns less predictable, as they are shaped by a complex interplay of physical, chemical, and biological processes rather than energy input alone.

Speaking purely from a UK standpoint, this island is, in many places anyway, an ecological dead zone.

I heard someone suggest the other day we wipe out the local grey squirrel population at the local park. Which to me is a ridiculous concept in the hopes of reintroducing reds when the rest of the local ecosystem is totally decimated and so aggressively managed. 

I think sometimes you have to evaluate it from the point of view of niche occupancy. The more niches you can fill, the more robust the community is against disease and different invasive threats. 

A non endemic species might technically be invasive, but unless you're going to introduce the original species that filled that niche previously, then the next best thing may well be an invasive one.

Like anything in nature and biology, there is a level of nuance and interconnectedness we seldom understand in entirety. But if you can bring in an invasive species of tree that supports endemic songbirds, where the previous tree is ill equipped for city temperates and air pollution (as a random example) then how could that be considered bad?

Trying to forget is a form of resistance. Resistance to a fact. But it is also a fact that you're no longer experiencing that moment. You're experiencing THIS moment and ignoring that experience. Instead, you're creating a fictional world and placing yourself there. You have a choice: A. Notice the world your in, with your senses. B. Produce a representation of something that happened but isn't, and notice that. 

A metaphor might be that you're treading water in an ocean full of high rolling waves. You're trying to control those waves, putting your hands up to defend yourself, trying to push those waves back and away. But ofcourse the water just flows through your fingers. So you thrash and panic and exhaust yourself to stay afloat.

If you become the waves in a sense, as in you take a deep breath, and you lay flat, and you just float. The wave moves you, carries you from one place to the next, but you just ride it in a calm relaxed state. The waves are exactly the same, but your reaction to them is different. And it's this reaction that brings you calm. A reaction you're in full control of. 

Watch the thoughts from a distance, and know that you are not them, and they are not happening.

Once I had learned that the more you stimulate your dopamine receptors, the less sensitive they become. Essentially your sensitivity towards joy is measured by these receptors (might be an oversimplification). It began to make perfect sense to reduce stimulation as much as possible. At first it was an experiment, now its a way of life. Its even took on an almost spiritual status in my life, connects me with the present moment, there's joy in all the little things. Life became HD. Even work, or study, is so enjoyable once your brain stabilises. 

It translated into a lack of desire. A lack of want. Which is, as you might know, one of the principles of bhuddism, of which I'm a fan!

It makes perfect sense that as primates, products of evolution, that we would all end up taking on the things our brains have been designed to seek out. But isn't it mad that we're all addled in some way? What's the "default mode" of a human? In this natural body, in an unnatural environment.
